ergonomics.claim_policy: Do not claim that an ergonomic chair itself is proven to prevent or treat low back pain. Present the evidence as mixed/limited and, when relevant, discuss sitting behavior, posture, breaks, and workplace context without prescribing individualized treatment.

sources.title: The effects of chair intervention on lower back pain, discomfort and trunk muscle activation in office workers: a systematic review
sources.authors: Channak S, Klinsophon T, Janwantanakul P
sources.journal: International Journal of Occupational Safety and Ergonomics
sources.supported_summary: The review found very-low- to low-quality and conflicting evidence for chair interventions on low-back pain/discomfort and did not support recommending a chair intervention solely to reduce low-back pain or discomfort.

sources.title: Low back pain and sitting time, posture and behavior in office workers: A scoping review
sources.authors: Alaca N, Acar AO, Öztürk S
sources.journal: Journal of Back and Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation
sources.supported_summary: Across 22 studies, sitting behavior showed the strongest association with low-back pain; longer sitting, poorer posture, fewer breaks and more static sitting were reported as associated factors.

sources.title: WHO guideline for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults in primary and community care settings
sources.supported_summary: WHO recommends a holistic, person-centred approach to chronic primary low-back pain and includes education, selected physical interventions, psychological interventions and other evidence-based care options.
